title: Checkpoint: What Religion Is
objective: After this level you can explain how scholars define, study and count religions without taking sides.
summary: From Tylor and Durkheim to van der Leeuw and Smart, scholars built tools to define, describe and count religions fairly. The chapter's toolkit, in order.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: you now carry a scholar's toolkit for any religion.
cards.body: Define carefully, describe fairly, date with care, count honestly. Let's lay the tools out in the order they were made, then use them.

cards.headline: How the study of religion grew

events.label: Tylor: religion as belief in spiritual beings
Van Gennep names rites of passage
Durkheim: religion unites a moral community
Van der Leeuw's classic phenomenology of religion
Smart becomes founding professor of religious studies at Lancaster
Smart's seven dimensions in The World's Religions

cards.headline: One toolkit, four jobs
cards.body: Each tool answers a different question. Definitions say what counts, and none fits every tradition. Smart's seven dimensions say what to look at, from rituals to sacred places, so the description stays balanced. Bracketing keeps it fair, and remembering that every tradition is a family of subtraditions keeps it accurate. Counting says how many, as long as you remember it measures what people report.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: How scholars describe any religion through seven dimensions without judging whether it is true.
Why religion is so hard to define, from Tylor's spiritual beings to Durkheim's moral community.
What ancient graves and Göbekli Tepe suggest about belief long before writing.
How researchers count the world's believers, and why unaffiliated doesn't mean unbelieving.

questions.prompt: Put these scholars' contributions in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Tylor came first in 1871, then van Gennep in 1909, Durkheim in 1912 and van der Leeuw in 1933.

questions.prompt: About 100,000 years ago, the youngster buried at Qafzeh had _____ placed on the chest.

options.label: a clay tablet with writing
options.rationale: Writing came tens of thousands of years later.

questions.explanation: Two deer antlers lay on the chest in what researchers call a deliberate, ceremonial burial.

questions.prompt: A student describes a temple's festivals, sacred stories and buildings without saying whether its teachings are true. Which two tools is she using?

options.label: Tylor's definition and a census count
Van Gennep's stages and a canon
Durkheim's definition and carbon dating
options.rationale: She's describing, not defining or dating.

questions.explanation: Festivals, stories and buildings are Smart's ritual, narrative and material dimensions; leaving truth aside is bracketing.

questions.prompt: What are van Gennep's three stages of a rite of passage, in order?
questions.explanation: Leave the old status, cross the threshold, join the community in a new one.

questions.prompt: A bat mitzvah and a Hindu antyeshti belong to different families of faith. What do they share?

options.label: Both are rites of passage marking a change of status
Both are forms of the Abrahamic covenant with God
options.rationale: Antyeshti belongs to the Indian family.

options.label: Both come from the Pali canon
Both are counted in the census
options.rationale: The point is what they do, not a count.

questions.explanation: Each moves people from one status to another: into religious adulthood, or through death and mourning.
